w: Diamond fever built an Edwardian town of 300 Germans in the Namib within a decade of a railway worker spotting a stone glinting in the sand in 1908. Richer fields further south drained it dry by the 1930s; abandoned by 1956, dunes have since poured through doors and windows, burying ballroom and bowling alley alike.
s: Diamond boomtown swallowed whole by desert sand
why: One of the world's most complete sand-reclaimed ghost towns

w: Sodium nitrate scraped from the driest desert on earth built an English-style town of nearly 4,000 workers, with a theatre, market and a pool cast from a ship's hull. Synthetic fertiliser and the Depression killed the trade; works closed in 1960 and stand untouched, a UNESCO-listed ghost town.
s: Nitrate boomtown left whole in the Atacama
why: Best-preserved nitrate mining ghost town on earth

w: Built in total secrecy under the codename Objekt 0774, this 3,000-square-metre, five-level bunker was Enver Hoxha's shelter against invasion and nuclear war, one of over 170,000 bunkers built across paranoid Communist Albania. Opened in 2014, its hundred concrete rooms now hold Cold War relics and art.
s: Dictator's five-storey doomsday bunker turned museum
why: The dictator's own nuclear-proof escape hatch, now public

w: Once the largest sulphur mine in Japan, this high-plateau complex housed over 15,000 workers in concrete blocks with then-luxurious central heating and flush toilets. Cheap refinery sulphur and falling demand bankrupted it by 1972. Acid drainage still bleeds pH-2 water, and fog often swallows the ruins whole.
s: Sulphur ghost town wrapped in permanent mist
why: Nicknamed Japan's real-life Silent Hill for its permanent mist

w: A future US president managed this Outback gold mine as a 23-year-old engineer in 1898, and the timber miners' cottages he oversaw still lean against the red dirt. Underground mining pulled 2.6 million ounces of gold before the shaft closed in 1963, emptying the town overnight and leaving it frozen mid-use.
s: Gold camp a young Herbert Hoover once ran
why: Ghost town once run by a future US president, Herbert Hoover

w: Second only to Potosi's Cerro Rico, this Andean silver mine once supported 60,000 people and ran Bolivia's first railway. A locomotive still in the yard was held up by Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid. Mining ended in 1959; roughly 400 residents now live among the rusting rolling stock and colonial mansions.
s: Silver boomtown Butch Cassidy's gang once robbed
why: Andean silver town robbed by Butch Cassidy's outlaw gang

w: Gold fever drew thousands of prospectors to this bushveld camp in the 1890s, but a richer reef found on the Witwatersrand and rampant malaria emptied it almost as fast as it filled. Named for a Boer state secretary, it now counts a handful of residents among crumbling facades and one surviving colonial hotel.
s: Malarial gold-rush town abandoned within a decade
why: Boomed and emptied within a decade of South Africa's gold rush

w: Balti stonemasons raised this fortress-palace in the 16th century for a prince who fled Baltistan after a failed assassination, its timber halls said to have held a wind-powered rotating chamber famed as far as Lhasa. Dogra conquerors dismantled it in the 19th century, leaving a shell above the village.
s: Ladakhi fortress with a legendary spinning room
why: Remote Himalayan fort said to have had a rotating room

w: Slate quarrymen and their families settled this steep valley from the 1810s, working a rock face above a dark tarn reached through a narrow tunnel. Failing quarries emptied the settlement by the 1940s; roofless cottages, a ruined chapel and barracks now ring Llyn Cwmorthin beneath still-active slate workings.
s: Slate quarrying village lost above a mountain lake
why: Roofless slate village hidden behind a mountain lake

w: Moscow-subsidised lead ore mining built this settlement deep in the Karatau mountains, its ore trucked 150 kilometres to a Shymkent smelter. Independence killed the subsidies; the mine closed and the town all but emptied, leaving stone barrack rows, a school and a still-tended mosque scattered across the arid hillside.
s: Soviet lead-mining town left to the Karatau wind
why: Soviet mining town emptied almost overnight after 1991

w: Radon-rich springs made this the USSR's premier spa, drawing 125,000 visitors a year to 22 grand sanatoriums built partly by German POWs in Stalinist-classical marble. Soviet collapse and the 1992 Abkhaz war left displaced families living in the crumbling colonnades, which still stand half palace, half refuge.
s: Stalin-era marble spa town, now half refugee shelter
why: Soviet spa palaces now doubling as refugee housing

w: Founded as a mining camp in 1578, this Andean city has been consumed from inside for a century by the Raul Rojas open pit, one of the largest urban mines on earth. Whole neighbourhoods like Ayapoto were relocated as the crater crept outward; guided viewpoints now overlook streets ending abruptly at the pit's edge.
s: Viewpoint over a city being eaten by its own mine
why: A 400-year-old city literally being swallowed by its mine

w: Moorish, then Portuguese, defenders held this hilltop above the Guadiana from the 10th century on, its star-shaped bastions among the grandest on the Alentejo frontier. A gunpowder magazine blast in 1911 gutted the fortress and church; ivy-choked ramparts and a roofless nave now overlook Spain.
s: Star-fort ruin staring across the Spanish border
why: Star-fort blown apart by its own gunpowder store in 1911

w: Chrysotile asbestos pulled from this pit built, then slowly consumed, the town once literally named Asbestos, its crater growing two kilometres wide and 370 metres deep as streets were moved to make way for it. Mining stopped in 2011; a lookout platform, ringed by asbestos-flecked rockery, now overlooks the void.
s: Two-kilometre asbestos pit swallowing its own town
why: A town renamed itself to escape the stigma of its own pit

w: Silver, gold and mercury mines around this borderland town once supported roughly 70,000 people through the Porfiriato boom. Flooding, revolution and falling ore prices emptied it by the early 1900s; crumbling haciendas, smelter ruins and open shafts sit half-reclaimed by scrub, artists slowly resettling the centre.
s: Silver mining town abandoned to cactus and quiet
why: Once-70,000-strong silver town now a near-empty adobe ruin

w: Quartz gold from the Blackwater Shaft supported over 600 residents through the 1930s, with a school, hospital and hall carved from West Coast bush. When the shaft flooded and collapsed in July 1951, the mine was abandoned outright and the town emptied within months, its foundations now walked by conservation trails.
s: Gold town abandoned within months of a shaft collapse
why: A whole town vanished within months of one shaft collapse

w: US Army engineers reshaped a rocky islet into a 350-foot concrete warship hull, armed with 14-inch naval guns, to guard the mouth of Manila Bay from 1914. Japanese troops held it through most of WWII until Americans pumped fuel into its vents and ignited it in 1945; the scorched hulk still sits offshore.
s: The concrete battleship guarding Manila Bay
why: An entire island rebuilt into the shape of a battleship

w: Copper hauled from this pit for roughly a thousand years once supplied two-thirds of Europe's demand and bankrolled Sweden's 17th-century wars. A Midsummer's Eve collapse in 1687 gouged out the vast crater still visible today. Mining ended in 1992; tours now descend the old fire-set tunnels of this UNESCO site.
s: Thousand-year copper pit that funded an empire
why: The copper pit that financed Sweden's age as a great power

w: Eleven hotels, a brewery and the region's first public pool served 3,500 gold miners at this boomtown's 1907 peak, with four trains daily from Kalgoorlie. The Cosmopolitan mine's decline emptied it through the century; fewer than 20 remain, and the surviving Grand Hotel still pours drinks among ruined streets.
s: 3,500-strong gold town now down to one open pub
why: Once 3,500 strong, now a living ghost town with one pub left

w: Black volcanic tuff walls raised by Russian imperial engineers in the 1830s garrisoned troops guarding the Ottoman frontier above what was then Alexandropol. Later Soviet use gave way to abandonment; roofless barrack blocks and gun emplacements stand open to the wind beside the Mother Armenia statue.
s: Tsarist fortress abandoned above a border city
why: Tsarist border fortress standing empty over Armenia's edge

w: Bosnian defenders hand-dug this 800-metre passage beneath the airport runway in three months during 1993, the only route out of a Sarajevo cut off by Serb forces for nearly four years. Up to 4,000 people and 30 tonnes of supplies moved through it daily; a short stretch survives beneath a private house turned museum.
s: Hand-dug lifeline that kept a besieged city alive
why: The secret tunnel that kept besieged Sarajevo alive

w: A herring-oil factory raised in 1934 became the largest concrete building in Iceland and Europe's first automated fish plant, its conveyor belts and cookers feeding a boom village of 260. The herring vanished by the late 1940s and the factory closed in 1954; caretakers now run a hotel beside its rusting machinery.
s: Iceland's largest concrete building, left to rust
why: Iceland's largest concrete building, now a rusting relic

w: A 1920s lakeside spa town of 1,500 residents drew 25,000 tourists a year for its supposedly healing waters, until a broken dike sent a ten-metre flood over it in 1985. Waters receded only after 2009, revealing a petrified, salt-white skeleton of hotels and trees, home to one former resident until his death in 2024.
s: Resort town that spent 25 years underwater
why: A resort town spent 25 years drowned, then resurfaced salt-white

w: The Glaoui clan built this High Atlas stronghold from 1860 with some 300 craftsmen laying zellij tile and carved cedar ceilings, wealth built on the caravan route and later collaboration with French rule. Independence in 1957 stripped the family's power; the palace's reception halls stand roofless above the village.
s: Warlord's palace abandoned after independence
why: A warlord's opulent palace stripped bare after independence

w: Greek colonists from Chalcis founded this settlement around 640 BC on a rock formation resembling a splayed hand, later fortified by Norman lords as a feudal seat. A violent 1783 earthquake and years of decline drove residents out by the 1960s; volunteers have since part-restored its stone lanes as a ghost village.
s: Five-fingered clifftop village emptied by earthquake
why: Ancient hand-shaped clifftop village, nearly lost to time
